Introduction section: 'To obtain optical sectioning, we used the 100-year-old idea of light sheet illumination, once termed ‘ultramicroscopy’.'
Results section: 'Using ultramicroscopy we imaged GFP expressing neurons in whole brains of previously described thy1-GFP-M transgenic mice.'

General_Description.Text: Ultramicroscopy is a technique that allows imaging of whole fixed mouse brains with cellular resolution by combining light sheet illumination with a special tissue clearing procedure. This method enables optical sectioning by illuminating the specimen from the side with a thin light sheet, thereby generating no out-of-focus light. The clearing procedure involves immersing the specimen in a medium with a refractive index matching that of protein, rendering the brain transparent. Ultramicroscopy is suitable for high-throughput phenotype screening of transgenic mice and can be used to visualize neuronal networks, dendritic trees, and spines in three dimensions.
Text_Reference: Introduction section: 'We modified ‘ultramicroscopy’ by combining it with a special procedure to clear tissue.'
Introduction section: 'We therefore developed an alternative technique that allows one to observe macroscopic specimens like whole brains with microscopic resolution.'

Introduction section: 'The principle is based on the immersion of the specimen in a medium with the same refractive index as protein. Because intra- and extracellular compartments then have equal refractive indices, light is no longer scattered but traverses the specimen unhindered.'
Results section: 'Using ultramicroscopy we imaged GFP expressing neurons in whole brains of previously described thy1-GFP-M transgenic mice.'

Discussion section: 'The approach presented here converts the microscope into an optical tomograph. The most important feature of ultramicroscopy is its ability to image macroscopic specimens with micrometer resolution.'

Tissue_Types.Text1: The method allows imaging of whole fixed mouse brains with cellular resolution and can be used to detect single GFP-labeled neurons in excised mouse hippocampi.
Text1_Reference: INTRODUCTION section: 'Here we present an approach that allows imaging of whole fixed mouse brains. We modified ‘ultramicroscopy’ by combining it with a special procedure to clear tissue. We show that this new technique allows optical sectioning of fixed mouse brains with cellular resolution and can be used to detect single GFP-labeled neurons in excised mouse hippocampi.'

Tissue_Types.Text2: Embryos and whole brains of young mice up to postnatal day 10 (P10) became completely transparent.
Text2_Reference: INTRODUCTION section: 'The results of clearing strongly depended on age. Embryos and whole brains of young mice up to postnatal day 10 (P10) became completely transparent.'

Tissue_Types.Text3: The method is applicable to specimens labeled by immunohistochemistry, such as mouse cerebellum.
Text3_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'Our method is also applicable to specimens labeled by immunohistochemistry. We labeled a mouse cerebellum with mouse anti–neu-N followed by biotinylated goat anti-mouse and streptavidin-Cy3.'

Tissue_Types.Text4: We were also able to visualize whole mouse embryos by autofluorescence.
Text4_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of mouse embryos and fruit flies': 'We were also able to visualize whole mouse embryos by autofluorescence.'

Tissue_Types.Text5: Ultramicroscopy can also be applied to the study of insects, such as D. melanogaster.
Text5_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of mouse embryos and fruit flies': 'Ultramicroscopy can also be applied to the study of insects. Using D. melanogaster, we could show that the entire body, including muscles and the optic lobes in the nervous system, becomes transparent in our clearing solution.'

Time_Consumption.Text1: To preserve optimal GFP fluorescence, it was important to keep clearing time as short as possible, about 6 hours for isolated hippocampi and about 2 days for whole brains.
Text1_Reference: RESULTS section: 'To preserve optimal GFP fluorescence we found that it was important to keep clearing time as short as possible, that is, about 6 h for the isolated hippocampi and about 2 d for whole brains.'

Fluorescence_Compatibility.Text1: To obtain images of dendrites and spines, it was absolutely essential that GFP fluorescence persisted during the procedure. In contrast to previous informed reports, we could preserve GFP fluorescence during clearing.
Text1_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'To obtain images of dendrites and spines, it was absolutely essential that GFP fluorescence persisted during the procedure...'

Fluorescence_Compatibility.Text2: To preserve optimal GFP fluorescence we found that it was important to keep clearing time as short as possible, that is, about 6 h for the isolated hippocampi and about 2 d for whole brains.
Text2_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'To preserve optimal GFP fluorescence we found that it was important to keep clearing time as short as possible...'

Text3_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'We labeled a mouse cerebellum with mouse anti–neu-N followed by biotinylated goat anti-mouse and streptavidin-Cy3 (Fig. 3b).'

Preservation_Stability.Text1: To preserve optimal GFP fluorescence, it was important to keep clearing time as short as possible, that is, about 6 hours for the isolated hippocampi and about 2 days for whole brains.
Text1_Reference: RESULTS section: 'To obtain images of dendrites and spines, it was absolutely essential that GFP fluorescence persisted during the procedure. In contrast to previous informed reports, we could preserve GFP fluorescence during clearing. To preserve optimal GFP fluorescence we found that it was important to keep clearing time as short as possible, that is, about 6 h for the isolated hippocampi and about 2 d for whole brains.'

Application.Text1: Ultramicroscopy combined with a special tissue clearing procedure allows imaging of whole fixed mouse brains with cellular resolution, enabling detection of single GFP-labeled neurons in excised mouse hippocampi.
Text1_Reference: Introduction section: 'We show that this new technique allows optical sectioning of fixed mouse brains with cellular resolution and can be used to detect single GFP-labeled neurons in excised mouse hippocampi.'

Application.Text2: Ultramicroscopy enables three-dimensional visualization of dendritic trees and spines of populations of CA1 neurons in isolated hippocampi.
Text2_Reference: Introduction section: 'We obtained three-dimensional (3D) images of dendritic trees and spines of populations of CA1 neurons in isolated hippocampi.'

Application.Text3: Ultramicroscopy is applicable to imaging anatomical details in fruit flies and mouse embryos using autofluorescence.
Text3_Reference: Introduction section: 'Also in fruit flies and in mouse embryos, we were able to visualize details of the anatomy by imaging autofluorescence.'

Application.Text4: Ultramicroscopy is suited for high-throughput phenotype screening of transgenic mice, benefiting the investigation of disease models.
Text4_Reference: Introduction section: 'Our method is ideally suited for high-throughput phenotype screening of transgenic mice and thus will benefit the investigation of disease models.'

Application.Text5: Using ultramicroscopy, the shape of the hippocampus in the whole brain preparation can be visualized using a GFP emission filter.
Text5_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'We could easily visualize the shape of the hippocampus in the whole brain preparation using a GFP emission filter.'

Application.Text6: Ultramicroscopy allows visualization of GFP-labeled neuronal somata and dendrites in the hippocampus through the overlying neocortex.
Text6_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'Furthermore, we could discern GFP-labeled neuronal somata and dendrites in the hippocampus through the overlying neocortex...'

Application.Text7: Ultramicroscopy can image strongly autofluorescent structures such as the primary and secondary barrel field in the whole brain of a mouse.
Text7_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of different sources of fluorescence': 'Using autofluorescence imaging we could also discern strongly autofluorescent structures such as the primary and secondary barrel field.'

Application.Text8: Ultramicroscopy can visualize fiber tracts in brains of mice older than P14 by detection of scattered light.
Text8_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'Additionally, in brains of mice older than P14, we were able to visualize fiber tracts, probably owing to myelination.'

Application.Text9: Ultramicroscopy is applicable to specimens labeled by immunohistochemistry, enabling virtual histology.
Text9_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of different sources of fluorescence': 'Our method is also applicable to specimens labeled by immunohistochemistry.'

Application.Text10: Ultramicroscopy can visualize the circulatory system, including blood capillaries, in whole mouse embryos using autofluorescence.
Text10_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of mouse embryos and fruit flies': 'We were also able to visualize whole mouse embryos by autofluorescence. The circulatory system, including blood capillaries, became especially apparent...'

Application.Text11: Ultramicroscopy can reconstruct the entire body of D. melanogaster by imaging autofluorescence, including muscles and optic lobes.
Text11_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of mouse embryos and fruit flies': 'Ultramicroscopy can also be applied to the study of insects. Using D. melanogaster, we could show that the entire body, including muscles and the optic lobes in the nervous system, becomes transparent in our clearing solution.'

Application.Text12: The most intriguing application of our technique lies in the analysis of neuronal networks in the brain.
Text12_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'The most intriguing application of our technique lies in the analysis of neuronal networks in the brain.'

Note.Text1: Image quality degraded somewhat upon focusing deeper into the sample.
Text1_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'Image quality degraded somewhat upon focusing deeper into the sample.'

Note.Text2: For large objects, it is mandatory to use two-sided illumination, as the excitation becomes less intense when the light sheet traverses a larger specimen.
Text2_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'For large objects, we found it mandatory to use two-sided illumination, as the excitation becomes less intense when the light sheet traverses a larger specimen.'

Note.Text3: In brains older than P14 light scattering starts to influence visualization.
Text3_Reference: RESULTS section, 'Imaging of neurons': 'This means that in brains older than P 14 light scattering starts to influence visualization.'

Note.Text4: Mouse brains older than 2 weeks cannot be imaged completely, as heavily myelinated structures such as thalamus and brain stem do not become transparent.
Text4_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'Mouse brains older than 2 weeks cannot be imaged completely, as heavily myelinated structures such as thalamus and brain stem do not become transparent.'

Note.Text5: Resolution somewhat degrades if one focuses deeper into the brain, probably due to residual variations of the refractive indices of the cleared tissue, which leads to diffraction of the emitted light.
Text5_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'Generally resolution somewhat degrades if one focuses deeper into the brain. Besides light scattering, this is probably due to residual variations of the refractive indices of the cleared tissue, which leads to diffraction of the emitted light.'

Note.Text6: The specimens show a distinct autofluorescence, which reduces the visualization depth for small details, such as spines, through the whole mouse brain.
Text6_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'Furthermore, the specimens show a distinct autofluorescence, which reduces the visualization depth for small details, such as spines, through the whole mouse brain.'

Note.Text7: Imaging of spines is only possible in excised hippocampi, although dendrites of granule cells in the hippocampus could be visualized through the overlying neocortex.
Text7_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'Presently imaging of spines is thus only possible in excised hippocampi, although dendrites of granule cells in the hippocampus could be visualized through the overlying neocortex.'

Note.Text8: Our images suffer from spherical aberration as we presently have to use objectives that are not corrected for use in oil.
Text8_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'Furthermore, our images suffer from spherical aberration as we presently have to use objectives that are not corrected for use in oil.'

Note.Text9: Our 3D reconstructions are presently limited by computer power.
Text9_Reference: DISCUSSION section: 'Our 3D reconstructions are presently limited by computer power, as our graphics processors can not handle more than 600 optical slices with high resolution.'
